production.text: Combined textile structures and camelid fiber preserve evidence of skilled making.

evidence.text: A regional comparison is more secure than a precise itinerary or named maker.

obligation.text: Rotating service, resettlement and textile work were distinct arrangements. Provisioning does not establish equal choice or returns; the selected tunic cannot be assigned a particular obligation without provenance.

name: Inca weaving: skill across highlands and coast
place: Peru; highland technique and coastal comparisons
geographicPrecision: Broad Peruvian regional locator; no precise findspot or full itinerary is asserted.

interval.label: Tunic catalogue range, 1450–1550 CE
interval.note: A broad object range crossing the C6/C7 boundary and Spanish conquest; not the lifespan of the Inca state.

question: How can the way cloth is made reveal connections?
summary: An Inca-attributed tunic joins skilled textile work to a larger question: how did households, specialists and state demands fit together? The finished garment and its broad date do not identify a worker’s obligations. Roads, stores, later accounts and household archaeology provide other evidence. They also expose differences between what authorities claimed, what people supplied and what particular communities could do.

sections.title: Start with the garment’s construction
sections.text: The Met describes two woven pieces sewn together, camelid hair, striped areas and a jagged design. It interprets parts of that design as added by needle darning rather than woven into the structure. Making cloth involved several decisions and skills, not decoration alone. The catalogue compares highland techniques with central-coast traditions. This is an attribution based on features; it does not provide the maker’s name, an exact findspot or the garment’s recorded path between regions.

sections.title: Work could be demanded in different ways
sections.text: Museum accounts explain mit’a as rotating labor required by the state. Agricultural work, road building and military tasks drew on people whose households also needed continuing care and production. Textile work could involve domestic makers and specialists; an obligation should not be imagined as the same job for everyone. The conceptual diagram separates household work, state demands and provisioning. It does not identify which arrangement produced this particular tunic.

sections.title: Roads and stores joined movement to authority
sections.text: NMAI describes official travelers, messengers and work parties using the roads, with ordinary travelers requiring permission. Flores Ochoa and Matos explain stores holding food and textiles as well as tools and weapons. Collecting, keeping and distributing supplies required continuing labor. Such arrangements could support workers and military forces while concentrating control. An institutional explanation is not proof that all households consented, received equal returns or avoided hunger.

sections.title: Household evidence complicates a total-control story
sections.text: At Yanawilka, a settlement of resettled laborers near Vilcashuamán, researchers studied starch on stone tools from four domestic structures. Their results include foods that could not all have grown locally. These traces indicate wider food connections even in an area of strong state presence. The authors leave open whether some foods moved through direct exchange or controlled traffic. This is a particular archaeological study, not the selected tunic’s excavation or a diet for every Inca subject.

sections.title: The object range crosses a political rupture
sections.text: The tunic’s 1450–1550 catalogue range extends across the Spanish invasion. It remains an object date, rather than the empire’s full lifespan or an exact production year. Later Indigenous criticism also matters: Guaman Poma’s manuscript addressed colonial exploitation and proposed reform. Its early-seventeenth-century perspective cannot be relabeled an eyewitness account of every preconquest textile workshop.

claims.text: The museum gives a 1450–1550 object range and interprets highland technique alongside coastal comparisons.

returnPrompt: What does a piece of clothing reveal that a list of rulers might miss?

deeperReading.title: Rotating service and resettlement are different
deeperReading.text: The Yanawilka study distinguishes mit’a, involving turns of service, from mitmaqkuna, communities resettled away from ancestral homes. Both could support imperial goals, but their consequences for household life differed. A temporary absence and a long-term relocation are not interchangeable. The article also discusses women assigned to textile and food work through state institutions. These categories help ask about constraint and skill without assigning a biography to an unprovenanced garment. Regional investigation is still necessary.

deeperReading.title: A plant trace is not an itinerary
deeperReading.text: The researchers analysed 53 stone tools; nine were tested in both recovery rounds. Those repeat analyses do not add nine independent tools. Starch identification uses modern comparison material, with possible indirect contact and contamination discussed explicitly. The interpretation of non-local foods concerns access, not a traced journey or a named trader. Even the authors’ conclusion leaves alternatives for how food moved. Archaeological observations can test an account of restricted travel while still leaving mechanisms unresolved.

deeperReading.title: Indigenous authorship belongs in its own context
deeperReading.text: Guaman Poma wrote and drew under colonial rule, criticizing exploitation and addressing proposals to a Spanish king. The Royal Danish Library describes Spanish text with Quechua passages. That audience and purpose shaped the work; Indigenous authorship does not make it a transparent transcript of earlier life. Here the library introduction has been consulted, not the entire manuscript. Reading selected original pages with appropriate language expertise is a next research task, rather than an achievement claimed by linking a digitization.

evidenceReading.title: Separate skill, obligation and observed household traces
evidenceReading.introduction: The garment, institutional explanations and a local excavation are related questions, not one continuous provenance.

items.label: A constructed textile
items.text: The catalogue describes separate woven pieces, seams and added pattern work.
items.interpretation: These features support discussion of skill, not identification of a worker’s consent or labor category.

items.label: Turning service into supplies
items.text: Museum accounts describe rotating work and stores used for several kinds of goods.
items.interpretation: Provisioning and obligation belong together, but equal returns cannot be assumed.

items.label: Food beyond the local environment
items.text: The Yanawilka authors identify non-local foods through starch analysis.
items.interpretation: They leave direct exchange and state-controlled movement as alternatives. The tunic has no demonstrated connection to this site.

familyActivity.title: Follow work that the finished cloth hides
steps: Find stripes, the jagged pattern and the neck opening in the tunic photograph.
Use the work diagram to name a task before the garment was finished and a separate task supplying people with food.
Explain why a beautiful garment does not tell us whether its maker could choose the work.
familyActivity.explanation: Visible skill and evidence of obligation answer different questions. We need other records to connect this garment to a particular worker.

limitations: No complete Guaman Poma manuscript or original-language chronicle consultation; workers’ voices remain mediated and regional.
Selected article sections, not independent starch identification, supplementary data analysis or a universal household model.
No exact maker, findspot, journey or state commission assigned to the tunic; no claim that all reciprocal obligations were equal or voluntary.

placeStudy.title: An Andean household study, separate from the tunic
placeStudy.description: Approximate locators orient Cusco and the Yanawilka/Vilcashuamán research region. They are not the selected tunic’s findspot or an inferred journey. No royal road or food route is traced; the tunic’s broader existing Peru point stays distinct.

points.label: Cusco — capital area
points.text: A religious and political center in the museum synthesis. This city-area locator does not place a particular weaving household.

points.label: Yanawilka — studied household settlement
points.text: Rounded from the article’s site coordinates. Four excavated domestic structures supplied tools for starch study; no connection to the Met tunic is demonstrated.

points.label: Vilcashuamán — provincial center
points.text: Approximate town-area locator near the study settlement. The article distinguishes the center, nearby stores and Yanawilka; these points do not reconstruct a surveyed ancient boundary.
